items.title: Dan Morgenstern interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, April 9, 2013
items.q: And so Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote and I and some of the other people who worked for us would take turns doing the program.

ctx.x: And actually, one of the reasons why I did that, although I didn’t start initially, was that I’ve done quite a lot of radio over time. I started out at WBAI in New York. And Gunther Schuller and Martin Williams had a program called “The Scope of Jazz.” And Martin had to bow out and he turned it over to me. And so, that was back in the sixties. Nat Hentoff was also in it. Gunther was the first one and then he moved to Boston. Anyway, it was

like a series, one hour jazz, a Sunday night broadcast. But then once I got with the Institute we started, when WBGO was the new jazz radio station in Newark back thirty- some years ago, they came to us at the Institute and asked us to do a weekly program, and we decided to call it “Jazz from the Archives.” And so Ed Berger and Vincent Pelote and I and some of the other people who worked for us would take turns doing the program. We started out, the station didn’t have very much. They had no record library. We of…
No kidding. And of the Grammys you received, would you have said yes, that was some of my best work?

items.title: Vincent Pelote interviewed by Monk Rowe, Orlando, Florida, February 25, 2017
items.q: One of the first things I told Dan Morgenstern when I knew he was the Institute of Jazz Studies Director was, you know how many records I’ve bought strictly on the fact that you said it was a great record?

ctx.x: You know you’re in the record store and you’re reading and you learn who writes, who do you agree with, so I’m going to buy this because this person says this thing about it.

Yep. One of the first things I told Dan Morgenstern when I knew he was the Institute of Jazz Studies Director was, you know how many records I’ve bought strictly on the fact that you said it was a great record? And he gets all sheepish and everything.
Yeah, I was just going to say, “Well I hope you liked them.”

items.title: Dan Morgenstern — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I couldn’t have done it at all with Ed, first of all, and then Vincent, who’s been – the three of us have been together for the whole stretch here

ctx.x: . . . SETA, which was a training program for – she was from Jamaica. She was a charming person who, again, caught on quickly. She had a great telephone manner. She was good at taking messages. She was well organized. Jeanette. She was very good in that position. We got Vincent a scholarship to go to library school at Rutgers. He became a librarian. We eventually – we were a freestanding unit at that point in time. We had an advisory board. It included Larry Ridley, whom I had known for a long time before coming…

an appropriate facility. That was a great step forward. It also gave us more visibility within Rutgers itself and with the outside world. There was a very nice piece done by the then New York Times jazz critic Peter Watrous on the Institute with a photograph of me with a bunch of instruments. We have a big collection of instruments that belonged to famous musicians. The collection has grown, I would think, by now at least six-fold from the time that Rutgers received it from Marshall Stearns. I don’t know if I…

Speaking of which, what a good segue. We want to talk about your recent award and inclusion in the great NEA Jazz Masters program. Can you talk about what that meant when you heard the news, and something about the ceremony?
